Octobass 由 J.A. Dubois 於1834年起草，約1850年在巴: The octobass was drafted by J. A. Dubois in 1834 and built around 1850 in Paris by the maker Jean-Baptiste Vuillaume, and it was first shown publicly on the international stage at the Great Exhibition in London in 1851. Berlioz, in the 1855 revision of his treatise on orchestration, affirmed its usefulness and urged its wide adoption, but it has been very little used; the only known work that requires it is Gounod's Messe solennelle de Sainte-Cécile. The Musée de la musique in Paris holds the only surviving original. Later instruments are in Phoenix, Vienna, Montreal and private collections; a replica made by Pierre Bohr for Nicola Moneta in 1995 added mechanical innovations, and in 2010 Jean-Jacques Pagès built one for the Montreal Symphony Orchestra, which is at present the only orchestra that owns and performs on the instrument.
Octobass（三弦低音提琴）是歐洲弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs: The octobass is a European chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322-71, a three-string bowed instrument larger than the double bass. Because the fingerboard is extremely long and the strings extremely thick, the player stops them with metal clamps worked by levers and pedals. It has never been made in quantity and composers have used it little; the only known work to call for it is Gounod's Messe solennelle de Sainte-Cécile, and the Montreal Symphony Orchestra uses one in performance.
低音提琴的琴身採用歐洲雲杉或挪威雲杉製作面板，以增強共鳴效果；琴身側板及背板則使: The body uses European spruce or Norwegian spruce for the top, which strengthens the resonance, while the sides and the back are of maple or another hardwood, which gives structural strength. The neck is of birch or maple, rigid enough to carry the huge body. The fingerboard is ebony or another hard wood. The strings are steel-core or gut-wound, and the three-string design gives a particular sound. The fine tuners and the pegs use brass or gold-plated metal fittings.
來源顯示，此樂器的首次國際公開亮相是在1851年倫敦世界博覽會；唯一已知使用它的: The source shows that the instrument's first public international appearance was at the Great Exhibition in London in 1851; the only known work to use it is Gounod's Messe solennelle de Sainte-Cécile of 1855, where it appears only in the Benedictus and the Agnus Dei, usually an octave below the double bass. The Montreal Symphony Orchestra is at present the only orchestra that owns the instrument and uses it in performance. 本樂器為弦鳴樂器，以弓拉奏，體積遠大於一般低音提琴，三根粗弦使其音高極低。來源記: The instrument is a chordophone played with a bow, much larger than an ordinary double bass, and its three thick strings make its pitch extremely low. The source records that the open strings can be tuned to C1, G1 and C2, an octave below the cello in the low register, comparable with a modern double bass that has the low C extension; the double bass of the time lacked that extension, so its bass lies lower than others of the family. Levers and pedals let each string cover a perfect fifth in semitones, and the top reaches G2. There is also a tuning of C0, G0 and D1, whose lowest fundamental is below 20 hertz but which can still be heard through its overtones. The source does not mention how the volume is controlled.

演奏時不直接以手指按弦，而是操作槓桿與踏板；槓桿帶動頸部上方特定位置的金屬夾，夾: It is played not by stopping the strings with the fingers but by working levers and pedals; the levers move metal clamps at set points up the neck, which grip the string to change the pitch, and the string is then sounded with the bow. The principle is the same as the double bass's, but the fingerboard is extremely long and the strings extremely thick, so a mechanism helps with stopping. The order is: first check the position of the metal clamps, then engage them with the lever or pedal, and finally draw the bow.
